subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography — Development and Globalisation Reading
subtitle: Reading comprehension on development, inequality, aid, trade, globalisation and sustainability.
description: This reading pack gives KS3 students short geography passages with retrieval, inference and explanation questions. The passages are grounded in development indicators, inequality, aid, Fairtrade, supply chains, TNCs and sustainable development.

data.sourceTitle: Why Development Is More Than Money
data.targetTitle: Why Development Is More Than Money
data.sourcePassage: Development means improvement in people's quality of life. Money matters because families and governments can spend it on housing, roads, schools, hospitals and clean water. However, income alone does not prove that everyone has a good life. A country may have a high average income while poorer groups still lack safe housing or healthcare. Geographers therefore use several indicators. GNI per person and GDP per person show economic activity and average income. Life expectancy, literacy rate and infant mortality show important social conditions. HDI is useful because it combines health, education and income, but it is still a national average and can hide inequality within a country.

questions.question: What does development mean in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Development means improvement in people's quality of life.

questions.question: Which three areas does HDI combine?
questions.modelAnswer: Health, education and income

questions.question: Why can a high average income be misleading?
questions.modelAnswer: It can hide inequality because some poorer groups may still lack services such as safe housing or healthcare.

questions.question: Explain why geographers use several development indicators rather than only GDP per person.
questions.modelAnswer: GDP per person mainly shows economic activity, while other indicators show health, education and living conditions. Using several indicators gives a more balanced view of development.

data.sourcePassage: Development is uneven because places have different physical, historical, economic, political and social conditions. Physical geography can help development when a place has fertile soils, reliable rainfall, rivers, natural resources or access to ports. It can make development harder when a place faces drought, flooding, steep mountains, disease risk or a landlocked location. History also matters. Colonialism changed trade patterns and resource control in many places, and some countries were pushed towards exporting raw materials rather than manufacturing higher-value goods. Conflict, high debt and poor governance can slow development, while education, healthcare, technology and fair investment can support it.

questions.question: Name one physical factor that can make development easier.
questions.modelAnswer: One physical factor is fertile soil, reliable rainfall, rivers, natural resources or access to ports.

questions.question: Which option is a historical factor mentioned in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Colonialism changing trade patterns

questions.question: How can conflict affect development?
questions.modelAnswer: Conflict can slow development by damaging services, reducing trade, discouraging investment and making farming, school and healthcare less safe.

questions.question: Explain why physical factors do not decide a country's future on their own.
questions.modelAnswer: Physical factors matter, but technology, planning, governance, investment, education and healthcare can reduce some physical challenges and create new opportunities.

data.sourcePassage: Aid is help given to people, communities or countries. Emergency aid is short-term help after a crisis, such as food, clean water, blankets and medicine after a flood or earthquake. Development aid is long-term support designed to improve quality of life, such as wells, schools, clinics, teacher training or vaccination programmes. Aid can save lives and reduce poverty, but it does not always work well. Problems can happen if aid does not reach the people who need it, if local people are not consulted, or if projects cannot be maintained after funding ends. A village water project is more sustainable when local people help plan it and are trained to repair pumps.

questions.question: Which example is emergency aid?
options: Food and clean water after a flood
questions.modelAnswer: Food and clean water after a flood

questions.question: Give one example of development aid from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include wells, schools, clinics, teacher training or vaccination programmes.

questions.question: Why might an aid project fail after funding ends?
questions.modelAnswer: It might fail if local people are not trained to maintain it, if spare parts are unavailable, or if the project was not planned with the community.

questions.question: Explain why involving local people can make development aid more sustainable.
questions.modelAnswer: Local people understand local needs and can help manage and maintain the project, so benefits are more likely to last after outside funding ends.

data.sourcePassage: Countries trade because they do not all produce the same things. An import is bought from another country, while an export is sold to another country. Trade can help development by creating jobs and earning income, but it can also increase inequality. Primary goods such as cocoa beans, coffee, cotton or copper are raw materials and often sell for lower prices than manufactured goods. In a chocolate supply chain, cocoa may be grown in Ghana or Cote d'Ivoire, processed and exported, then turned into chocolate in another country. Fairtrade tries to give cocoa farmers a fairer deal through minimum prices, a Fairtrade premium, safer conditions and environmental standards. However, not all farmers can join Fairtrade schemes.

questions.question: What is an import?
questions.modelAnswer: An import is a good or service bought from another country.

questions.question: Which item is a primary good?
questions.modelAnswer: Cocoa beans

questions.question: Why do manufactured goods often sell for more than primary goods?
questions.modelAnswer: Manufactured goods include added value from labour, technology, design, branding, packaging and processing.

questions.question: Evaluate Fairtrade as a way to reduce inequality in cocoa supply chains.
questions.modelAnswer: Fairtrade can reduce inequality by supporting minimum prices, community premiums and safer conditions, but it is limited because not all farmers can join and it does not solve all global trade problems.

data.sourceTitle: How Global Supply Chains Link People
data.targetTitle: How Global Supply Chains Link People
data.sourcePassage: Globalisation is the increasing connection between places through trade, transport, technology, culture, finance and migration. A T-shirt sold in the UK may use cotton grown in one country, be sewn in another, shipped through ports and sold online to a customer in Britain. This shows interdependence because consumers, farmers, factory workers, transport companies and retailers depend on each other. Transnational corporations organise many global supply chains because different places offer raw materials, skilled workers, cheaper labour, transport links or nearby markets. Globalisation can create jobs, spread technology and give consumers more choice. It can also cause low wages, poor working conditions, pollution, carbon emissions and waste if supply chains are not managed fairly and sustainably.

questions.question: What is a TNC?
options: A company that operates in more than one country
A charity that only gives emergency aid
questions.modelAnswer: A company that operates in more than one country

questions.question: How does the T-shirt example show interdependence?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows that consumers, cotton farmers, factory workers, transport companies and retailers in different places depend on each other.

questions.question: Explain why globalisation can bring both benefits and problems.
questions.modelAnswer: Globalisation can create jobs, spread technology and increase choice, but it can also cause low wages, poor conditions, pollution, emissions and waste if rules are weak.
